# vocab.design

> A linked visual dictionary of design and UI vocabulary: terms, definitions, aliases,
> relations between concepts, and pointers to real implementations. Content is CC BY 4.0.

## When to use this

Reach for vocab.design when a task turns on which word names an interface thing.

- Naming a component, a pattern or a state before building it, in the word the rest of
  the industry already uses for it.
- Settling a loose word someone reached for: whether a "popup" is a modal, a popover, a
  toast or a tooltip, and what each of those claims.
- Resolving an alias to the term it names, before it goes into a spec, a ticket or a
  commit message. /snackbar and /toast are one entry.
- Reading what a term asserts, with a worked demo of it, instead of inferring the
  meaning from the name.
- Walking outward from a word already in hand: its variants, its parts, the words it
  gets confused with, and the design systems that ship it.

It defines words. It is not an implementation reference, an accessibility ruling, or
the current API of any design system; each term links out to the systems that
implement it.

## How to call it

- The whole vocabulary in one request: /llms-full.txt for every term with its
  definition, /terms.json for the same terms with their aliases, relations, tags and
  implementations.
- One term, with the word in hand: /{slug}.md is that term as raw markdown, frontmatter
  included. A slug is the headword lowercased with hyphens for spaces. An alias has an
  HTML page at /{alias} and no markdown twin, so resolve it to a slug first.
- Whether a word exists at all: /paths.json maps every slug to its headword and every
  alias to the term it resolves to. It is a fraction of terms.json and answers that one
  question on its own.
- A term found by description rather than by name: match against the definitions in
  /llms-full.txt. /search is a page rather than an API, so there is nothing to query.

Everything is static, public and CC BY 4.0. No key, no rate limit, no POST.

## Pages

The site is at https://vocab.design, and every path below is relative to it.

- /{slug}: a term. Definition, article, live demo, aliases, related terms, and the
  design systems that implement it.
- /{slug}.md: the same term as raw markdown.
- /{alias}: a redirect to the term that spelling names. Aliases live at the root beside
  the terms, so /snackbar answers as well as /toast.
- /browse/{category}: every term in one category, with definitions.
- /tags/{tag}: every term carrying one tag, grouped by category.
- /glossary and /glossary/{letter}: A to Z over every term and every alias.
- /search?q={query}: full text over headwords, aliases, definitions and articles,
  filtered by category and by tag.

## Data

- [llms-full.txt](https://vocab.design/llms-full.txt): all 1,124 terms with their definitions.
- [terms.json](https://vocab.design/terms.json): the whole dataset, including aliases,
  relations, tags and implementations.
- [rss.xml](https://vocab.design/rss.xml): the hundred most recently published terms.

## Categories

Every term has exactly one, and it is the kind of thing the term is.

- component (208): A named piece of interface you can point at, place, and reuse.
- layout (143): How a page arranges its regions, and what governs the arrangement.
- pattern (161): A recurring answer to a recurring problem, larger than any one component.
- aesthetic (65): A named visual style, with a period and a set of moves.
- interaction (85): What a reader does, and how the interface answers.
- motion (100): Change over time, and the vocabulary for describing it.
- typography (118): Type, and the measurements and conventions that set it.
- color (89): Colour as a system: palettes, roles, contrast, and schemes.
- surface (21): The finish on a shape: its corners, its edges, its depth, its texture.
- accessibility (134): Terms that exist so an interface works for everyone.

## Tags

Cross-cutting groupings. A term carries any number of them, or none.
Three tags are also terms, with a definition and a page of their own at /{tag}: dark-pattern, microinteraction, responsive-web-design.

- a11y (12): Terms filed under their own kind that exist because of accessibility.
- ai (12): The vocabulary of interfaces an assistant drives, or that drive one.
- assistive-tech (61): The software that reads an interface out, and the ways people drive it.
- auth (18): Signing in, staying in, and proving you are a person.
- canvas (24): An unbounded workspace, panned and zoomed, with things placed on it.
- commerce (25): Choosing, paying, and the pressure applied along the way.
- consent (10): Permission asked for, and the ways it is manufactured.
- content-design (57): The words in the interface, chosen as carefully as the pixels.
- dark-pattern (17): Every deceptive pattern that declares the term, from confirmshaming to the roach motel.
- dataviz (30): Charts and the parts they are assembled from.
- depth (54): Making a flat screen read as raised, layered, or three dimensional.
- design-tools (23): Vocabulary that comes from the tools designs are drawn in.
- devtools (12): Vocabulary that comes from the tools software is built with.
- dragging (43): Picking something up, moving it, and letting it go.
- editorial (59): Vocabulary the page inherited from print and publishing.
- email (15): Designing for an inbox, and for the renderers mail arrives in.
- errors (38): Something went wrong, and the ways back out of it.
- fonts (60): The files type arrives in, and what they can do.
- forms (68): Assembling a form, filling it in, and telling someone it is wrong.
- gamification (9): Progress, streaks, and rewards used as motivation.
- grids (37): Columns, rows, and the structure a page is laid against.
- i18n (14): Scripts, directions, and languages other than the one it was drawn in.
- icons (25): Small drawings standing in for words.
- illustration (32): Drawn artwork inside an interface, and the styles it is drawn in.
- keyboard (41): Reaching and driving an interface without a pointer.
- media (38): Video, audio, images, and the controls and alternatives they need.
- menus (39): A list of commands, opened from something.
- messaging (22): Conversations, presence, and things that arrive unannounced.
- microinteraction (16): The loops that are kinds of one, and the ripples and toasts that are parts of one.
- navigation (49): Getting somewhere else, and knowing where you are.
- onboarding (17): The first run, the empty screen, and teaching in place.
- overlays (49): Surfaces that open over the page, and how they give it back.
- perceived-performance (34): Making a wait read as shorter than it is.
- perception (118): How eyes and attention actually take an interface in.
- platform-registers (56): Vocabulary that exists because of one platform: TV, watch, phone, desktop, headset.
- pointer (44): What a mouse or a pen can do that a finger cannot.
- progress (21): How far along something is, and how much of it is left.
- responsive-web-design (6): LukeW's layout patterns, the five ways a page reflows as the viewport narrows.
- retro (50): Looks borrowed from an earlier era, on purpose.
- screen-size (39): Designing for a screen whose size you do not know.
- scroll (42): Everything that happens because a page is longer than a screen.
- search (16): Asking for something by typing, and narrowing what comes back.
- selection (20): Marking what an action will apply to.
- sound (17): Interfaces that are heard: speech, alerts, and audio.
- spacing (36): The empty room between things, and the scales it comes from.
- tables (18): Rows, columns, and reading across both.
- text-editing (19): Writing and editing text in place.
- theming (36): One interface, more than one palette.
- time (20): Dates, clocks, calendars, and saying when.
- tokens (46): Design decisions stored as names so they can be repointed.
- touch (55): Input from a finger rather than a cursor.
- wcag (49): Terms that are, or come straight from, a WCAG success criterion.
- web-platform (93): Terms that name a web platform feature, not a design idea.
- windowing (34): Windows, panes, and the frame around an application.
